scout.purpose: A developer must be able to locate a project, run a tool, interpret its result, and change files deliberately instead of treating the computer as a collection of opaque windows.
scout.realWorldUse: Gradle, adb, Git, emulators, build logs, and continuous integration all expose command-line interfaces even when Android Studio provides a graphical front end.
scout.outcome: Navigate paths, distinguish files from directories, run a command with arguments, and explain working directory, exit status, standard output, and standard error.

sections.title: A path locates an item in a directory tree

blocks.text: A filesystem organises named files inside directories. An absolute path begins at the filesystem root and identifies one location independently of the current directory. A relative path begins from the process working directory. The dot segment means the current directory and two dots mean its parent. Before editing or deleting anything, print the working directory and list the target. Spaces are part of a name, so quote a path such as "My Project" rather than allowing the shell to split it into two arguments. File extensions are conventions that help tools and people; the file content remains the decisive evidence.

blocks.code:
pwd
ls
cd "My Project"
ls src
# ./gradlew refers to gradlew in the current directory
blocks.caption: Each relative name is resolved from the shell working directory. Quoting preserves a path containing spaces as one argument.

blocks.title: Path forms
rows: Relative path from the working directory
Executable named gradlew in the current directory

sections.title: A command starts a process with arguments

blocks.text: The shell parses a command line into a program name and ordered arguments. It then starts a process, an executing instance of that program. Environment variables provide inherited configuration, while command flags select behaviour for one invocation. Standard input supplies data, standard output carries normal results, and standard error carries diagnostics. These are streams, not promises about whether work succeeded. Read the program exit status as well: zero normally means success and a non-zero value identifies a failure category. Never paste an unfamiliar command into a terminal until you can identify its executable, arguments, targets, and side effects.

blocks.code:
node --version
npm run validate
echo $?  # exit status of the previous command in many shells
blocks.caption: node and npm are executables; the remaining tokens are arguments. The final status communicates success separately from printed text.

steps.label: Parse
steps.detail: Shell turns text into a program and arguments.

steps.label: Start process
steps.detail: Operating system creates an executing process.

steps.label: Exchange streams
steps.detail: Process reads input and writes output or diagnostics.

steps.label: Exit
steps.detail: Process returns a numeric status to its caller.

blocks.text: Command-line confidence comes from a repeatable safety loop. Establish context with pwd, inspect names with a directory listing, and ask a tool for help before guessing flags. Prefer a read-only command first. Make the smallest intended change with an exact path, then rerun inspection or tests to verify the outcome. Tab completion reduces spelling mistakes and command history helps reproduce work, but both can repeat a dangerous target quickly. Recursive deletion, broad globs, administrator privileges, and commands downloaded from the internet deserve an explicit pause because they can affect far more than one file. A terminal is powerful because it is precise; supply that precision yourself.

blocks.code:
pwd
find content/lessons -name "level-01-week-04-*.json" -maxdepth 1
npm run test:content
blocks.caption: The sequence establishes context, performs a read-only targeted inspection, and asks the project test to verify content.

blocks.title: Resolve the target first
blocks.text: Do not run a destructive command against an unresolved variable, broad directory, or pattern you have not inspected.

trap_check.mistake: Running a command from the wrong working directory.
trap_check.why: Relative paths resolve somewhere different and may change or fail against the wrong files.
trap_check.fix: Print the working directory and inspect the exact target first.

trap_check.mistake: Treating printed output as proof of success.
trap_check.why: A program can emit diagnostics and still return a failing status.
trap_check.fix: Read the exit status and verify the intended artifact or state.

challenge_intro.task: Write a small shell checklist or script that confirms it is inside the DroidQuest data directory, reports relevant JSON file counts, and runs content validation without modifying files.
challenge_intro.successLooksLike: The working directory is checked before relative paths are used. A failed validation produces a non-zero final status. The script performs no destructive operation.

recall.prompt: How does a relative path get its starting point?
recall.answer: It is resolved from the current working directory of the process.
A running instance of a program with arguments, environment, streams, and an exit status.

recall.prompt: What does exit status zero normally mean?
recall.answer: The command completed successfully according to its contract.
